paper_a.title: Phase Transition of the Largest Eigenvalue for Non-null Complex Sample Covariance Matrices (Baik, Ben Arous, Peche, 2005)

paper_b.title: On the Distribution of the Length of the Longest Increasing Subsequence (Baik, Deift, Johansson, 1999)

metadata.description: BBP extends BDJ's Tracy-Widom universality result from null (identity covariance) to spiked covariance matrices. BDJ established that the Tracy-Widom distribution $F_2$ governs the largest eigenvalue of GUE and the longest increasing subsequence. BBP shows that $F_2$ still governs the subcritical regime, but a phase transition occurs when population spikes exceed $1 + \sqrt{\gamma}$, yielding Gaussian fluctuations for outlier eigenvalues and new generalized TW distributions at criticality.

matches.explanation: Both papers use the Tracy-Widom distribution $F_2$ as the fundamental limiting law. BDJ defines it as the GUE edge limit (Painleve II formula). BBP uses exactly the same $F_2$ in the subcritical case and generalizes it to a family $F_{2,r}$ at criticality.

Both prove Tracy-Widom limits for largest eigenvalues. BDJ: the longest increasing subsequence (equivalently, the null Wishart/LUE largest eigenvalue) has $F_2$ fluctuations at the edge $2\sqrt{n}$ with scale $n^{1/6}$. BBP subcritical: the spiked Wishart largest eigenvalue has $F_2$ fluctuations at the Marchenko-Pastur edge $\lambda_+$ with scale $n^{-2/3}$. BBP's result reduces to (a matrix-model analog of) BDJ when all spikes equal 1 (no spikes). BBP is the strict extension.
BBP's supercritical phase (outlier eigenvalues with Gaussian fluctuations at $\sqrt{n}$ rate) is entirely new, with no BDJ counterpart. BDJ's null setting has no mechanism for eigenvalue separation.
BBP's critical case with generalized Tracy-Widom distributions $F_{2,r}$ is a genuinely new family of distributions not appearing in BDJ.

The spiked covariance model (population covariance with finitely many eigenvalues different from 1) is the central new object introduced by BBP, with no BDJ counterpart. BDJ works in the null (identity covariance / uniform permutation) setting.

The BBP phase transition threshold $\ell^* = 1 + \sqrt{\gamma}$ is a new phenomenon. It delineates when a signal (spike) is strong enough to be detectable from the largest eigenvalue. No counterpart in BDJ.
BBP's high-dimensional regime $p/n \to \gamma$ is specific to the sample covariance / spiked model setting. BDJ works in the single-parameter $n \to \infty$ regime (permutations of size $n$).

The longest increasing subsequence of random permutations is the combinatorial object central to BDJ, with no direct BBP counterpart (though BBP's last passage percolation application is related via the RSK correspondence).

BDJ's Poissonization and Gessel-identity approach to the determinantal structure is specific to the permutation/LIS problem. BBP uses different techniques (direct analysis of the Wishart kernel) to access the Tracy-Widom limit.

Both papers rely on Riemann-Hilbert steepest descent methods for asymptotic analysis, though applied to different kernels. BDJ: Bessel kernel from Poissonized LIS. BBP: Laguerre kernel from the spiked Wishart matrix. The analytical framework is shared even though the specific RH problems differ.

BBP's applications to last passage percolation with perturbed weights and queueing theory are specific to the spiked extension, though last passage percolation in the unperturbed case is closely related to BDJ's LIS.
BDJ's moment convergence result has no explicit BBP counterpart stated, though moment convergence likely holds in the BBP subcritical case as well.

BDJ's reference to the Vershik-Kerov/Logan-Shepp law of large numbers $\ell_n / \sqrt{n} \to 2$ is specific to the LIS context and has no BBP counterpart (the BBP analog would be the Marchenko-Pastur law for the bulk).
